title: SpaceX Catches Starship Mid-Air in Historic First as NASA Eyes Moon Return

# SpaceX Catches Starship Mid-Air in Historic First as NASA Eyes Moon Return


By OpenTools Team


·


November 16, 2026


SpaceX's Starship upper stage completed 14 laps around Earth and returned to be caught mid‑air by the launch tower's mechanical arms — a first in spaceflight history. The 22‑hour mission deployed 26 Starlink satellites while the booster failed its own catch attempt. NASA, which is paying billions for Starship to land astronauts on the moon, called it "almost magic."


## Caught Mid-Air After 22 Hours in Space


SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier. According to the[Associated Press](https://abcnews.go.com/Technology/wireStory/spacexs-starship-returns-orbit-captured-launch-pad-arms-138148467) , the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad in Texas, nestling into the tower's "chopstick" arms in what SpaceX called the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space.


The world's largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX's Starbase near the U.S.-Mexican border. The upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit, released 26 advanced Starlink satellites, and completed 14 laps around Earth at 165 miles (265 kilometers) in altitude. "Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted during the landing webcast, according to the[Associated Press](https://abcnews.go.com/Technology/wireStory/spacexs-starship-returns-orbit-captured-launch-pad-arms-138148467) . "Look at her! Baby, she's back!"


## Booster Falls Short, Ship Delivers


SpaceX aimed for a dramatic double catch — bringing both the Super Heavy booster and the Ship upper stage back to the launch tower. It didn't happen with Super Heavy.[Space.com](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/whats-next-for-spacexs-starship-after-epic-flight-15-chopsticks-catch) reports that the booster diverted to a Gulf of Mexico splashdown after experiencing a low-fuel alarm. Its guidance system sensed it wasn't in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.


But the upper stage delivered. Catching Ship is tougher and riskier than catching Super Heavy — the upper stage flies much higher and faster, making its return trip far more involved. SpaceX had caught Super Heavy on three previous test flights but had never even attempted a Ship catch before Saturday.


- **Super Heavy booster** Diverted to Gulf of Mexico after low-fuel alarm — engines stopped too soon on descent


- **Ship upper stage** First-ever mid-air catch of a Starship returning from orbit — 22.5 hours after liftoff


- **Flight 15** SpaceX's 15th full-scale Starship test flight since 2023, only its second trip to orbit


## NASA: 'Almost Magic'


Calling it an "epic day," Elon Musk ascended the launch tower after the catch to take up-close video with his phone and even hugged the spacecraft. "Looks great," he reported via X. But the significance goes far beyond one test flight. NASA is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base.


"It was almost magic," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X, as reported by[the AP](https://abcnews.go.com/Technology/wireStory/spacexs-starship-returns-orbit-captured-launch-pad-arms-138148467) . "Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to the moon."


> "It was almost magic. Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to the moon."


**Jared Isaacman** - NASA Administrator


## Full Reusability, Finally


Saturday's catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. The double catch — booster and ship — will be standard on operational missions, enabling rapid inspection, refurbishment, and reflight.[Space.com](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/whats-next-for-spacexs-starship-after-epic-flight-15-chopsticks-catch) notes that Elon Musk has said SpaceX is targeting 10,000 Starship launches per year by 2030 — more than one liftoff every hour on average.


The company has yet to demonstrate rapid reflight. It has reflown Super Heavy boosters on two occasions, but several months separated each reuse. Now that Ship recovery is proven, the path to true rapid reuse is clearer. SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months — the starting point for NASA's next Artemis mission.


## Why This Matters Beyond SpaceX


The Starship architecture underpins several of SpaceX's most ambitious projects. The company wants its next-gen Starlink V3 broadband network to consist of 100,000 satellites, and its planned Starmind AI data-center constellation would feature one million spacecraft. For perspective: the current Starlink network in low Earth orbit is about 11,000 satellites strong, according to[Space.com](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/whats-next-for-spacexs-starship-after-epic-flight-15-chopsticks-catch) .


The reusability milestone also affects NASA's Artemis timeline. Artemis III's four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with both Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV — humanity's first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago. Catching Starship from orbit isn't just a spectacle. It's the key that unlocks the entire Artemis program.
